stances.claim: The two senior dissenters (Leonen and Caguioa) are correct in arguing for liberal interpretation — the Court should not use 'technicalities to conveniently justify its dismissal' and evade its obligation as the final arbiter on validity of legislative and executive acts; waiting for the Senate to rule formally on its jurisdiction is 'trivial and vain' when constitutionality is substantively at stake.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban defends Senate President Migz Zubiri's chime that the Supreme Court's 13-2 dismissal in Senate v. Medialdea (promulgated July 5, 2022, released recently -- with 'DISMISSED' rendered in 'all caps and bold fonts in original') 'does not in any way diminish or disturb long-established doctrines on the legislative's power to conduct inquiries in aid of legislation.' His thesis: the Senate is substantively right but procedurally wrong. The undisputed facts: the COA's 2020 Annual Audit Report noted a deficiency in the accounting of over P67 billion intended for COVID-19 emergency, prompting a Senate blue ribbon committee investigation focused on DOH disbursements; then-President Duterte complained of 'browbeating' of executive officials, prompting then-Executive Secretary Medialdea's memorandum prohibiting their appearance for 'strict compliance.' The Senate challenged the memorandum before the Court. Justice Amy C. Lazaro-Javier's ponencia held that the Senate's own Rules of Procedure 'effectively proscribes a premature resort' to certiorari because the upper chamber failed to first resolve the executive's stance that only the Joint Congressional Oversight Committee under the Bayanihan Acts had jurisdiction; under the Rules of Court, the Senate also failed to demonstrate the absence of an 'appeal or any other plain, speedy, and adequate remedy' -- that remedy being the Senate's Internal Rules. Panganiban classifies this as 'the strict or verba legis method of interpretation,' notes that the two most senior dissenters (Leonen and Caguioa) argued for liberal interpretation -- Caguioa stressing that the Court should not use 'technicalities to conveniently justify its dismissal' and that it is 'trivial and vain' to wait for the Senate to rule formally on its jurisdiction when constitutionality is substantively at stake -- and aligns himself, 'in the mold of United States Justice John Marshall Harlan,' with the great dissenters. He closes by reaffirming Senate v. Ermita (April 20, 2006), one of 'the four most important pillars of the Panganiban court I am personally proud of,' which 'unanimously and courageously thrashed Executive Order No. 464' and held the inquiry power 'coextensive with the power to legislate' -- subject only to bounded executive privilege over confidential military and diplomatic matters and presidential conversations with subordinates, with the SC's own internal deliberations reciprocally protected under separation of powers. As a rule, however, under transparency and accountability principles, 'the extraordinary character of the exemptions... inclines heavily against executive secrecy and in favor of disclosure.'
